source_text: Οὕτω Χριστῷ προσάγεται, οὕτω πρὸς Χριστὸν μετατίθεται, ὁ πολὺς ἐν ἀσεβείᾳ, καὶ πλείων ἐν εὐσεβείᾳ Κυπριανὸς, ὁ μέγας καὶ διώκτης καὶ στεφανίτης, ὁ τὴν μετα βολὴν οὐχ ἧττον ἢ τὴν ἀρετὴν θαυμάσιος. Οὐ γὰρ οὕτω μέγα τύπον ἀγαθοῦ διασώσασθαι, ὡς τὸ καινοτομῆσαι θεοσέβειαν. Τὸ μὲν γὰρ τῆς συνηθείας, τὸ δὲ τῆς εὐβουλίας· καὶ τὸ μὲν τῶν πολλοῖς ὑπαρ χόντων, τοῦ δὲ ὀλίγα τὰ παραδείγματα. ΙΖʹ. Ἀλλ' οἷον δὴ κἀκεῖνο τῶν ἐκείνου θαυμάτων; Μικρὸν ἔτι τῷ λόγῳ προσκαρτερήσωμεν, ἵνα τῷ ἀθλητῇ χαρισώμεθα. Τοιαύτη μὲν ἡ τοῦ ἀνδρὸς πολιτεία, τοιοῦτος δὲ ὁ τῆς ἀθλήσεως τρόπος. Ἐπεὶ δὲ καταλύει τὸν βίον (εἰ θέμις τοῦτο εἰπεῖν, ἀλλὰ μὴ πρὸς Θεὸν ἐκδημίαν ὀνομάσαι τὸ ἐκείνου πρᾶγμα, ἢ πόθου πλήρωσιν, ἢ δεσμῶν λύσιν, ἢ βάρους διάζευξιν), θαυματουργεῖταί τι κἀνταῦθα τῶν προειληφότων ἄξιον· τὸ μὲν ὄνομα πολὺ παρὰ πᾶσι Κυπριανοῦ, καὶ οὐ Χριστιανοῖς μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς τὴν ἐναντίαν ἡμῖν τεταγμένοις (πᾶσι γὰρ ὁμοίως τὸ καλὸν αἰδέσιμον)· τὸ σῶμα δὲ ἀφανὲς ἦν, καὶ ὁ θησαυρὸς παρά τινι γυναίῳ τῶν θερμῶν εἰς εὐσέβειαν, καὶ τοῦτο ἐπὶ μακρόν· οὐκ οἶδ' εἴτε τιμῶντος τοῦ Θεοῦ τὴν φιλόθεον, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο περιεχομένην τοῦ μάρτυρος, εἴτε τὸν πόθον ἡμῶν γυμνάζοντος, εἰ μὴ φέροιμεν ζημιούμενοι, καὶ τῶν ἁγίων λειψάνων ἀποστερούμενοι. Ἐπεὶ δὲ οὐκ ἠνέσχετο τὸ πάντων ἀγαθὸν ἴδιον ποιῆσαί τινος ὁ τῶν μαρτύρων Θεὸς, οὐδὲ τὸ κοινὸν ζημιῶσαι τῇ πρὸς ἐκείνην χάριτι, δημοσιεύει τὸ σῶμα δι' ἀποκαλύψεως, καὶ ταύτην γυναίῳ τινὶ τῶν ἀξίων τὴν τιμὴν καταθέμενος· ἵν' ἁγιασθῶσι καὶ γυναῖκες, ὥσπερ τὸν Χριστὸν καὶ τεκοῦσαι πρότερον, καὶ τοῖς μαθηταῖς ἀπαγγείλασαι μετὰ τὴν ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀνάστασιν, οὕτω καὶ νῦν Κυπριανὸν, ἡ μὲν παραδείξασα, ἡ δὲ παραδοῦσα τὸ κοινὸν ὄφελος. Τοῦτο τῶν ἐκείνου καλῶν τὸ τελευταῖον. Οὕτως εἰς μέσον ἔρχεται ὁ τοῦ μὴ λαθεῖν ἄξιος, καὶ οὐ συγχωρεῖται φιλοσοφῆσαι τὴν ἑαυτοῦ κλοπὴν, ἐπειδὴ καὶ τῶν ἐπὶ τοῖς σώμασι τιμῶν κρείσσων ἐκεῖνος καὶ ὑψηλότερος. ΙΗʹ. Τὰ μὲν οὖν παρ' ἡμῶν τοσαῦτα, καὶ οὐκ οἶδ', ὅτι δεῖ πλείονα λέγειν. Οὐδὲ γὰρ, εἰ μακρὸν ἀποτείναιμεν λόγον, εἴποιμεν ἄν τι τῶν ἐκείνῳ προσόντων ἄξιον, καὶ ὧν ἕκαστος περὶ τοῦ ἀνδρὸς ὑπείληφεν. Καὶ ταῦτα, ὅσον ἀφοσιώσασθαι τὴν ὀφειλομένην ἐκείνῳ τιμὴν, διήλθομεν· τὰ δὲ λοιπὰ παρ' ὑμῶν αὐτῶν προσθετέον, ἵνα τι καὶ αὐτοὶ τῷ μάρτυρι προσενέγκητε, τὴν τῶν δαιμόνων καθαίρεσιν, τὴν τῶν νόσων κατάλυσιν, τὴν τοῦ μέλλοντος πρόγνωσιν· ἃ πάντα δύναται Κυπριανοῦ καὶ ἡ κόνις μετὰ τῆς πίστεως, ὡς ἴσασιν οἱ πεπειραμένοι, καὶ τὸ θαῦμα μέχρις ἡμῶν παραπέμψαντες, καὶ τῷ μέλλοντι παραδώσοντες χρόνῳ. Μᾶλλον δὲ τὰ μείζω τούτων προεισενέγκατε, καὶ οἷα τοὺς ἐκεῖνον γνησίως τιμῶντας εἰκὸς, σώματος κένωσιν, ψυχῆς ἀνάβασιν, κακίας ἀποφυγὴν, ἀρετῆς ἐπίδοσιν· αἱ παρθένοι τὴν ἀσαρκίαν, αἱ γυναῖκες τὴν εὐκοσμίαν ἀρετῆς μᾶλλον ἢ σώματος, οἱ νέοι τὴν κατὰ τῶν παθῶν ἀνδρίαν, οἱ πρεσβῦται τὴν εὐβουλίαν, οἱ ἐν δυναστείᾳ τὴν εὐνομίαν, οἱ ἐν στρατηγίᾳ τὴν ἡμερότητα, οἱ ἐν λόγοις τὸ εὔλογον· εἴπω τι καὶ τῶν ἡμετέρων, οἱ ἱερεῖς τὴν μυσταγωγίαν, οἱ τοῦ λαοῦ τὴν εὐπείθειαν, οἱ ἐν πένθει τὴν παράκλησιν, οἱ ἐν εὐημερίᾳ τὸν φόβον, οἱ πλούσιοι τὴν μετάδοσιν, οἱ πένητες τὴν εὐχαριστίαν· πάντες τὴν κατὰ τοῦ πονηροῦ καὶ πικροῦ διώκτου παράταξιν, ἵνα μὴ φαινόμενος βάλλῃ, μὴ τοξεύῃ κρυπτόμενος, μὴ ὡς σκότος πολεμῇ, μὴ ὡς ἄγγελος φωτὸς παίζῃ, καὶ κλέπτῃ πρὸς τὸ τῆς ἀπωλείας βάραθρον.
thought_title: Cyprian's hidden body revealed for the common good
orientation: Gregory has just described Cyprian's beheading and now turns to the wonder of how his hidden body was later revealed by God.
pass_a_gloss: Thus to Christ he is brought, thus toward Christ he is converted, the great in impiety and greater in piety Cyprian, the great both persecutor and crown-winner, the one wonderful not less for the change than for the virtue. For it is not so great a thing to preserve a model of good as to innovate godliness. For the one belongs to habit, the other to good counsel; and the one belongs to things existing among many, but of the other the examples are few. 17. But what sort of thing indeed is that other one of his wonders? Let us persist a little longer with the word, in order that we may gratify the athlete. Such was the man's way of life, and such was the manner of the contest. But when he ends his life (if it is lawful to say this, but not to name his deed a departure to God, or a fulfillment of longing, or a loosing of bonds, or a separation from burden), something worthy of the things previously received is worked as a wonder also here: the name of Cyprian was great among all, and not among Christians only, but also among those arrayed against us (for to all alike the good is worthy of reverence); but the body was unseen, and the treasure was with some woman of those fervent in piety, and this for a long time; I do not know whether God was honoring the God-loving woman, and for this reason she was holding fast to the martyr, or whether he was exercising our longing, if we should not bear being deprived and being robbed of the relics of the saints. But when the God of the martyrs did not endure that the good of all be made the private possession of someone, nor to harm the common good by the favor toward that woman, he makes the body public through a revelation, and this honor he laid upon some woman of the worthy ones; in order that women also might be sanctified, just as formerly both giving birth to Christ, and announcing him to the disciples after the resurrection from the dead, so also now Cyprian, the one woman showing him forth, the other handing over the common benefit. This is the last of his good things. Thus into the midst comes the one worthy of not being hidden, and he is not permitted to philosophize his own theft, since also he is better and higher than the honors paid to bodies. 18. The things from us then are so many, and I do not know that it is necessary to say more. For not even if we should stretch out a long speech would we say anything worthy of the things belonging to him, and of the things which each person has supposed about the man. And these things we have gone through, as much as to discharge the honor owed to him; but the remaining things must be added by you yourselves, in order that you also may offer something to the martyr: the destruction of demons, the dissolution of diseases, the foreknowledge of the future; all of which things even the dust of Cyprian can do with faith, as those who have experienced know, both having sent the wonder down to us, and being about to hand it over to future time. But rather bring in advance the things greater than these, and such as is fitting for those who genuinely honor him: emptying of body, ascent of soul, avoidance of evil, increase of virtue; the virgins the fleshlessness, the women the orderliness of virtue rather than of body, the young men the courage against passions, the old men the good counsel, those in power the good order, those in command the gentleness, those in words the reasonableness; let me say something also of our own things, the priests the initiation into mysteries, those of the people the obedience, those in mourning the consolation, those in prosperity the fear, the rich the sharing, the poor the thanksgiving; all the battle array against the evil and bitter persecutor, in order that he may not strike when appearing, may not shoot when hidden, may not wage war as darkness, may not play as an angel of light, and may not steal toward the pit of destruction.

choices.why: The glossary gives 'conversion' for μετάθεσις; the verb here describes Cyprian's change toward Christ, so 'is converted' keeps the glossary sense.
The glossary gives 'crown' for στέφανος; στεφανίτης is the one who wins the crown, so 'crown-winner' preserves the martyrdom imagery.
The glossary gives 'contest' for ἄθλησις; 'of the contest' keeps the martyrdom metaphor of athletic struggle.
The glossary gives 'relics' for λείψανα; 'of the relics' preserves the technical sense of the martyr's bodily remains.
The dust of Cyprian's relics is said to work wonders; 'dust' is the literal sense and fits the relic context.
The term refers to the priestly role of leading others into the sacred mysteries; 'initiation into mysteries' keeps the cultic sense.

pass_b_english: So Cyprian is brought to Christ; so he is converted toward Christ—Cyprian, who was great in impiety and greater still in godliness, the great persecutor and crown-winner, a man no less admirable for his conversion than for his virtue. For it is not so great a thing to preserve the pattern of goodness as it is to make godliness something new. The one belongs to habit, the other to sound judgment; the one is found in many people, but of the other there are few examples.

But what about this other wonder of his? Let us linger a little longer on the account, so that we may give a gift to the athlete. Such was the man's way of life, and such was the manner of his contest. And when he ended his life—if it is right to say this, rather than to call what happened to him a departure to God, or a fulfillment of longing, or a release from bonds, or a separation from a burden—something worthy of what had gone before was worked as a wonder even here. The name of Cyprian was on everyone's lips, and not only among Christians but also among those arrayed against us, for what is good is equally revered by all. But his body was hidden, and the treasure was kept by a certain woman fervent in piety, and this for a long time. I do not know whether God was honoring her love for Him, and for that reason she was holding fast to the martyr, or whether He was training our longing, in case we could not bear to suffer loss and be deprived of the relics of the saints.

But the God of martyrs did not allow the good of all to become the private possession of one person, nor did He permit the common benefit to be diminished by His favor toward her. He made the body public through a revelation, entrusting this honor to a certain woman among the worthy, so that women too might be sanctified. Just as women first gave birth to Christ and then announced Him to the disciples after His resurrection from the dead, so now one woman revealed Cyprian and another handed over the common benefit. This is the last of his good deeds. So the man who deserved not to be hidden comes into the open, and he is not permitted to make a philosophy of his own theft, since he is greater and higher than the honors paid to bodies.

These things, then, are what we have to offer, and I do not know that more needs to be said. For even if we stretched out a long speech, we could not say anything worthy of what belongs to him and of what each person has understood about the man. And we have gone through these things only so far as to discharge the honor owed to him. The rest you must add from yourselves, so that you too may bring something to the martyr: the overthrow of demons, the destruction of diseases, the foreknowledge of what is to come. All these things even the dust of Cyprian can do together with faith, as those who have experienced it know—those who have passed the wonder down to us and will hand it on to the time to come.

But rather, bring forward things greater than these, the things that befit those who honor him genuinely: emptying of the body, ascent of the soul, flight from evil, increase in virtue. Let virgins bring their freedom from the flesh, women their good order in virtue rather than in the body, young men their courage against the passions, elders their sound counsel, those in power their respect for law, those in command their gentleness, those skilled in words their reasonableness. And let me say something of what belongs to us: let priests bring their guidance in the mysteries, the laity their obedience, those in mourning their consolation, those in prosperity their fear, the rich their generosity, the poor their gratitude. Let all bring their battle array against the evil and bitter persecutor, so that he may not strike when he appears, may not shoot his arrows while hidden, may not wage war as darkness, may not play as an angel of light and steal people away to the pit of destruction.

problems.quote: she held fast to the martyr
problems.why: Source means 'withholding/concealing the martyr's body,' not 'held fast to.' The body was being kept hidden.
problems.fix: she was withholding the martyr's body
problems.ruling: περιεχομένην τοῦ μάρτυρος means 'being enclosed/keeping concealed the martyr' (body as object); 'held fast to' misleads by making her the subject clinging to him, reversing the concealment sense.

problems.why: In context of priests, μυσταγωγία means conducting/initiating others into mysteries (the sacraments), not receiving initiation. The English reverses agency: priests perform mystagogy for others, they don't undergo it.
problems.ruling: μυσταγωγία = priests' conducting/initiating others into mysteries, not their own 'initiation into mysteries.' Agency reversed.

edits.old: she held fast to the martyr
edits.new: she was withholding the martyr's body

edits.old: let priests bring their initiation into mysteries
edits.new: let priests bring their guidance in the mysteries

fixed: Changed 'she held fast to the martyr' to 'she was withholding the martyr's body' because περιεχομένην τοῦ μάρτυρος means she was keeping/concealing the martyr's body, not clinging to him.

Changed 'let priests bring their initiation into mysteries' to 'let priests bring their guidance in the mysteries' because μυσταγωγίαν refers to the priestly act of initiating others into the mysteries, not receiving initiation.

problems.quote: if it is right to say this, rather than to call what happened to him a departure to God, or a fulfillment of longing, or a release from bonds, or a separation from a burden
problems.source_quote: εἰ θέμις τοῦτο εἰπεῖν, ἀλλὰ μὴ πρὸς Θεὸν ἐκδημίαν ὀνομάσαι τὸ ἐκείνου πρᾶγμα, ἢ πόθου πλήρωσιν, ἢ δεσμῶν λύσιν, ἢ βάρους διάζευξιν
problems.why: The parenthesis prefers those names over saying he ended his life; English ranks “ended his life” above them.
problems.fix: if it is right to say this, and not rather to call what befell him a departure to God, or a fulfillment of longing, or a release from bonds, or a separation from a burden
problems.ruling: Source "ἀλλὰ μὴ ... ὀνομάσαι" means 'rather than name it a departure to God...' (preferring those names). English "rather than to call" reverses the preference, misleading the reader.

problems.quote: he is not permitted to conceal his own theft by philosophy
problems.source_quote: οὐ συγχωρεῖται φιλοσοφῆσαι τὴν ἑαυτοῦ κλοπήν
problems.why: φιλοσοφῆσαι means to treat his theft as philosophy, not to hide it by means of philosophy.
problems.fix: he is not permitted to make a philosophy of his own theft
problems.ruling: φιλοσοφῆσαι τὴν ἑαυτοῦ κλοπήν means to make his theft a matter of philosophy/rationalize it; "conceal by philosophy" changes the meaning.

last_rejected.why: πλείων means 'more' not 'greater'; contrast is quantity not degree.
last_rejected.ruling: πλείων means 'more/greater'; 'greater' is within normal range for comparative of πολύς in qualitative contexts.

last_rejected.why: κένωσις here means 'emptying' in sense of fasting/abstinence, not kenotic self-emptying; 'emptying of the body' is unclear.
last_rejected.ruling: σώματος κένωσιν literally means 'emptying of body'; whether ascetic or kenotic, rendering is within normal range and not misleading.
